title: Neat and messy: why a falling leaf never lands in the same place twice

summary.text: Drop a crumpled ball of paper ten times, and it lands near the same spot every time. Drop a flat paper leaf the same way, and it lands somewhere new each time. Both are pulled down by gravity, and the air pushes against both. The air pushes the light, flat leaf so much that the smallest change sends it somewhere else. Splashes, falling leaves and clouds are like this: they follow rules, but they never happen the same way twice. A kolam drawn from dots is the other kind of thing. It has order, so you can draw it the same way every morning.
summary.art: A child standing on a newspaper on the floor, letting go of a flat paper leaf that flutters sideways, while a crumpled paper ball falls straight down onto a circle drawn on the paper. Around the circle are many crayon crosses where the leaf landed before.

intro.hook: Try this. Tear two pieces of paper the same size. Crumple one into a tight ball. Hold both up high and let go at the same moment. Which one lands right under your hand? Do it again. Did the flat one land in the same place as last time?
intro.text: Some things happen the same way every time. The Sun rises in the east, and a ball of paper falls straight down. Other things never happen the same way twice. A falling leaf, a splash of water and the shape of a cloud are always new. In this unit you find out why. You test a flat paper leaf and a paper ball, make splash prints with haldi water and draw a kolam. You also learn what scientists mean by order and chaos, and find out that even messy things follow rules.
intro.art: Two hands held up high, one letting go of a crumpled paper ball and the other a flat piece of paper. The ball falls straight down and the flat paper swings from side to side.

outcomes: By the end I can say what order and a pattern are, and find neat and messy things in my home.
By the end I can show that a flat paper leaf lands in a new place each time, but a paper ball does not.
By the end I can say that gravity pulls a falling leaf down and the air pushes it, so tiny changes send it somewhere new.
By the end I can show that splashes are never exactly the same, even from the same drop and the same height.
By the end I can say that messy happenings still follow rules, even when we cannot say what will happen.
By the end I can say what scientists still argue about: is anything truly random?

terms.meaning: Order is when things are arranged by a rule, so you can say where each one goes or what comes next.
terms.example: Pencils lined up from shortest to longest are in order. A kolam drawn around a grid of dots has order too.
terms.art: Six pencils in a row on a table, from the shortest on the left to the longest on the right.

terms.meaning: A pattern is something that repeats in the same way, again and again.
terms.example: Red, blue, red, blue on a border of a saree is a pattern. So is the beat in a song you clap along to.
terms.art: A strip of cloth with a border of red and blue triangles repeating along it.

terms.meaning: Messy means there is no rule you can use to say where each thing is.
terms.example: Rajma beans tipped out of a tumbler land in a messy heap. Nobody can say where each bean will be.
terms.art: A steel plate with rajma beans scattered across it in an uneven heap.

terms.meaning: Chaos is a word scientists use for things that follow rules but still never happen the same way twice. A tiny change at the start makes a big change at the end.
terms.example: A falling leaf is chaotic. Let go of it a tiny bit differently, and it lands far from the last place.
terms.art: A paper leaf drawn falling in a wavy zig-zag line, with three dotted paths showing it could land in three different places.

terms.meaning: To predict is to say what will happen before it happens.
terms.example: You can predict that a crumpled paper ball will land right under your hand.
terms.art: A girl pointing at a spot on the floor before she drops a paper ball, with a thought bubble showing the ball landing there.

terms.meaning: Gravity is the force that pulls things down towards the Earth.
terms.example: When you let go of a spoon, gravity pulls it down to the floor.
terms.art: A spoon falling from a hand towards a kitchen floor, with an arrow pointing down.

terms.meaning: Air resistance is the push of the air against something moving through it.
terms.example: Open your hand flat and wave it fast. You can feel the air push back. That push is air resistance.
terms.art: A child waving an open, flat hand through the air, with small curved lines showing the air pushing on the palm.

terms.meaning: A splash is what happens when a liquid hits something hard and flies outwards in drops.
terms.example: A raindrop hitting a steel bucket makes a splash.
terms.art: A drop of water hitting a flat surface and spreading out into a crown of tiny droplets.

explanations.concept: Order and patterns: neat things follow a rule
explanations.context: This card explains what makes something neat, or ordered.
explanations.definition: Order is when things are arranged by a rule. If you know the rule, you can say where each thing goes, or what comes next. A pattern is order that repeats.
explanations.description: When you line up pencils from shortest to longest, you are using a rule. Anyone who knows the rule can make the same line again. A kolam is the same. In Tamil Nadu and many other places, people draw kolams at the doorstep by looping lines around a grid of dots. The dots and the rules let them draw the same kolam again tomorrow. Messy things have no rule we can use. When you tip rajma beans onto a plate, nobody can say where each bean will be.
examples: Pencils lined up from shortest to longest
A kolam drawn around a grid of dots
A saree border of red, blue, red, blue
Steel tumblers stacked one inside another
explanations.art: On the left, a neat kolam of loops around five rows of dots. On the right, a heap of rajma beans scattered on a plate.

explanations.concept: Why a falling leaf never lands in the same place twice
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the paper leaf test.
explanations.definition: A falling thing is pulled down by gravity and pushed by air resistance. A flat, light thing is pushed so much by the air that it swings, turns and slides as it falls. Tiny changes in how it starts change where it ends.
explanations.description: In the paper leaf test, the paper ball and the paper leaf were made from the same paper. They weighed the same. The ball pushed through the air and fell almost straight down. The flat leaf had a big, flat side for the air to push on. So it swung and slid from side to side. You can never let go of a leaf in exactly the same way. It may tip a tiny bit more, or the air may move a tiny bit. Those tiny changes grow as the leaf swings, so it lands in a new place. The leaf still follows the same rules as the ball. It is just much harder to predict.
examples: A dry leaf falling from a tree
A paper leaf in the test landing somewhere new each time
A sheet of newspaper sliding off a table and gliding across the floor
explanations.art: Two paths from the same hand: a short straight line for the paper ball, and a long zig-zag for the flat paper leaf, each ending at a cross on the floor.

explanations.concept: Why no two splashes are the same
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the splash test.
explanations.definition: When a drop hits a flat surface, it spreads out very fast into a thin ring. The edge of the ring breaks into tiny droplets that fly outwards. Where it breaks depends on tiny wobbles in the drop and tiny bumps on the surface.
explanations.description: In the splash test, you dropped the same yellow water from the same height. Each splash had a different number of little dots around it, in different places. No drop is a perfect ball. Each one wobbles a little as it falls. Paper also has tiny bumps you cannot see. These tiny differences decide where the edge of the splash breaks into droplets. Drops from higher up hit harder, so they spread further and break into more dots.
examples: A splash of haldi water on paper
Raindrops on a steel bucket lid
Water dripping from a tap into a steel plate
Milk splashing as it is poured into a tumbler
explanations.art: Four splash prints in yellow on white paper, each a round middle with little dots around it, all a different shape.

explanations.context: This card puts the leaf test and the splash test together.
explanations.definition: A thing can follow exact rules and still be impossible to predict. This happens when tiny changes at the start grow into big changes at the end. Scientists call this chaos.
explanations.description: People often think that if something is messy, nothing is in charge of it. It is just luck. But the paper leaf and the splash both followed rules every time. Gravity pulled them down. The air pushed them, and the water spread out. The rules did not change. What changed were tiny things we cannot see or control. Weather, clouds and waves are chaotic too. Weather scientists can say what is likely in the next few days, but not exactly what will happen a month from now.
examples: Smoke curling up from an agarbatti
explanations.art: A falling paper leaf with two small arrows on it: one pointing down marked gravity, and one pointing up marked air.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about.
explanations.description: Something is random if nothing at all decides how it comes out. The leaf and the splash follow rules, so they are not truly random. We just cannot see the tiny things that decide them. But is anything in the world truly random? Scientists still argue about this.
examples: How a coin lands when you toss it
Which way a tiny particle of light goes when it hits glass

perspectives.who: Pierre-Simon Laplace, a French scientist, in 1814
perspectives.explanation: He wrote that if a mind knew where every tiny particle was, and every push on it, it could predict everything. So nothing is truly random. It only looks random because we do not know enough.
They say that the tiniest particles, smaller than atoms, behave in ways that are truly random. Even knowing everything, you could only say what is likely.
They say there may be hidden rules even for the tiniest particles, that we have not found yet. Nobody has settled this.

explanations.art: A girl looking at a falling leaf through a magnifying glass, with a question mark beside her.

agreed.text: Gravity pulls every falling thing down, and the air pushes against it as it falls.
agreed.evidence: In the paper leaf test, both landed on the floor. The flat leaf took longer and swung about, because the air pushed on its big flat side.

agreed.text: A flat, light thing like a leaf or a feather lands in a different place almost every time it falls.
agreed.evidence: In the paper leaf test, the crosses for the leaf were spread across the paper. The crosses for the ball were bunched near the middle.

agreed.text: No two splashes are exactly the same, even from the same drop and the same height.
agreed.evidence: In the splash test, each splash had a different number of little dots, in different places. Scientists filming splashes very fast see the same thing.

agreed.text: Some things follow exact rules and still cannot be predicted, because tiny changes grow. Scientists call this chaos.
agreed.evidence: Weather follows the rules of air, water and heat. Yet weather scientists can say what will happen only a few days ahead, because tiny changes in the air grow over time.

challenging.claim: Splashes make neat crowns, with the points spaced evenly.
challenging.who: Arthur Worthington, an English scientist, believed this for many years from his drawings of splashes, made in the late 1800s.
challenging.for: When he saw splashes in a flash of light, they looked like neat crowns with evenly spaced points.
challenging.against: When he took photographs of splashes in the 1890s, they were far less even than his drawings. He had drawn them neater than they really were, without meaning to.
challenging.context: This card is about a scientist whose eyes saw more order than there really was.

challenging.claim: A leaf falls wherever luck sends it, and no rules decide where it lands.
challenging.for: Nobody can say where a falling leaf will land, so it seems to be pure luck.
challenging.against: Gravity and the air push the leaf by the same rules every time. Scientists who study falling paper with computers can work out how it will swing, if they know exactly how it started.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea that messy means no rules.

challenging.claim: With a big enough computer, we could predict exactly where every falling leaf will land.
challenging.for: The leaf follows rules, so a computer that knew everything about the leaf and the air could follow them.
challenging.against: Nobody can measure every tiny movement of the air and every tiny bend in the leaf. The smallest mistake grows as the leaf falls.
challenging.context: This card is about whether chaos could ever be predicted.

big_questions.q: The paper ball and the paper leaf were made of the same paper. Why did only one of them land in the same place each time?
big_questions.hint: What was different about their shapes? Where could the air push?

big_questions.q: Suppose you could let go of the paper leaf in exactly the same way, with the air exactly the same. Would it land in the same place?
big_questions.hint: Do the rules change from one drop to the next, or does something else change?

big_questions.q: Is a messy room just a room where nobody has decided where things go?
big_questions.hint: Think of the rajma beans on the plate. Did anything decide where each bean went?

big_questions.q: If the future cannot be known exactly, is that a good thing or a bad thing?
big_questions.hint: Think of a game whose ending you always know. Would it still be fun?

big_questions.q: Every falling leaf and every splash is new. Is anything in the world ever exactly the same twice?
big_questions.hint: Think of today's breakfast, the sky this morning, and yourself.

how_we_found_out.story: Splashes happen too fast to see. In the 1870s, an English scientist called Arthur Worthington found a way to look at them. In a dark room, he let a drop fall. Just as it hit a plate, an electric spark flashed for a tiny moment. In that flash, he saw the splash for an instant, and then drew it from memory. He did this many times. His drawings showed splashes as neat crowns, with points spaced evenly all around, like a pattern. Then, in the 1890s, Worthington began taking photographs of splashes in the flash. When he looked at the photographs, he was surprised. The real splashes were much less even than his drawings. The points were different sizes and not evenly spaced. Without meaning to, he had drawn them neater than they really were. He wrote about this honestly. It taught scientists that our eyes and memory like to see order, even where there is less of it.
how_we_found_out.who: Arthur Mason Worthington, an English physicist
how_we_found_out.when: Drawings from the 1870s, photographs from the 1890s, his book 'A Study of Splashes' in 1908
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That splashes are neat, even shapes. Photographs showed that real splashes are uneven, and that Worthington's drawings had made them look neater.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in old-fashioned clothes in a dark room, looking at a drop falling onto a plate lit by a bright spark, with a sketchbook of neat splash drawings beside him.

story.title: Nila and the Flowers That Would Not Listen
story.note: Nila, Paati and Kannan are made up. Paati is a Tamil word for grandmother.
text: Nila was eight, and she lived in Madurai with her Paati and her little brother Kannan. Kannan was five.
Every morning, before the sun was hot, Paati swept the step outside their front door. She sprinkled it with water. Then she drew a kolam with white rice flour.

First, Paati made dots. Five dots in a row, then five more below them, then five more, until there was a square of dots. Then she let the flour run from her fingers in a thin white line. The line looped around each dot and came back to where it started.
Nila sat on the step and watched. 'How do you always know where the line goes?' she asked.
'There is a rule,' said Paati. 'The line goes around every dot, and it never touches a dot. If you keep the rule, the kolam comes out the same every time.'

Nila tried. Her first kolam had a wobbly line, and one loop was too fat. But by the end of the week, she could draw a small kolam with nine dots. She drew it on Monday. She drew it again on Tuesday. It looked the same both days.
'That is because a kolam has order,' said Paati. 'Order means there is a rule. Anyone who knows the rule can make it again.'
Next to their house grew a big champa tree, with white and yellow flowers. Every morning a few flowers fell onto the step.

One morning, Kannan had an idea. 'I will make the flowers fall right in the middle of Nila's kolam,' he said. He climbed onto the low wall, picked up a fallen flower and held it over the middle dot. He let go.
The flower spun round and round, slid sideways and landed near the edge of the step.
'Again!' said Kannan. He held the flower in the very same place. He let go. This time the flower turned the other way and landed on Nila's foot.
Kannan tried ten times. The flower never landed in the same place twice. Not once did it land in the middle.
'It is not listening to me!' said Kannan, and he stamped his foot.
Nila thought about it. Then she went inside and came back with a little ball of rice flour dough from the kitchen. She gave it to Kannan. 'Drop this,' she said.
Kannan held the dough ball over the middle dot and let go. Plop. It landed right on the middle dot. He tried again. Plop. Right on the middle again.
'The dough listens and the flower does not,' said Kannan. 'Why?'

Nila picked up the flower. It was light, and its petals were wide and flat. 'Feel this,' she said, and she waved the flower quickly through the air. 'The air pushes on the flat petals. So the flower swings about as it falls. The dough ball is small and round. The air cannot push it about so much.'
'But I let go of the flower the same way every time,' said Kannan.
'Nearly the same way,' said Nila. 'Your fingers can never be exactly the same. And the air is always moving a tiny bit. A tiny change at the top makes a big change at the bottom.'
Just then, big drops of rain began to fall. Paati, Nila and Kannan ran inside and watched from the doorway.

The raindrops landed on the step. Each one made a small splash, with tiny drops flying out all around. Nila looked carefully. No two splashes looked the same. Some had many tiny drops around them, and some had only a few.
The rain washed away part of the kolam, so the white lines became messy streaks.
Kannan looked sad. 'Your kolam is gone,' he said.
'That is all right,' said Nila. 'I know the rule. I can draw it again tomorrow, exactly the same.' She smiled. 'But nobody in the whole world can make the rain splash the same way twice.'
Paati laughed. 'The rain has rules too,' she said. 'Every drop falls down and every drop splashes out. It is only that the tiny things that decide each splash are too small for us to see.'

The next morning, Nila drew her kolam again, and it came out the same as before. Then she showed Kannan how to make the dots, and how the line goes around every dot. And when a champa flower fell onto the step, they both watched to see where it would land. Neither of them could guess.
story.epiphany: A kolam has order, so it can be drawn the same way again by following the rule. A falling flower and a splash follow rules too, but tiny changes we cannot see make them different every time.
ask: Why could Nila draw the same kolam on Monday and on Tuesday?
Why did the dough ball land on the middle dot, but the flower did not?
Kannan said he let go of the flower the same way every time. Was he right? Why?
Paati said the rain has rules too. What rules does a raindrop follow?
What would you drop to make it land in the same place every time?

A small boy standing on a low wall, letting go of a white and yellow champa flower above a kolam, while the flower spins sideways.
A boy dropping a small dough ball that lands right on the middle dot of a kolam, and his older sister smiling beside him.

The next morning: the girl showing her little brother how to draw the line around the dots, and a flower falling from the tree above.

experiments.title: The Paper Leaf Test: where will it land?
experiments.context: In this experiment you cut two leaf shapes from the same paper. You crumple one into a ball and keep the other flat. You drop each one ten times from the same height, and mark where it lands.
experiments.question: If we drop a flat paper leaf and a paper ball from the same height, will each land in the same place every time?
experiments.predict: Look at the flat leaf and the paper ball. When we drop them ten times each, which one will land inside the plate circle more often? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both come from the same sheet of paper and are the same size, so they weigh the same. We drop both from the same height, holding them over the same spot. We switch off the fan and close the windows, so moving air does not spoil the test. We drop each one ten times, because one drop can be a fluke.
results_table: Paper ball: inside or outside the circle?
Paper leaf: inside or outside the circle?

materials.item: one sheet of notebook paper or printer paper
a steel plate, to draw a circle around
two crayons or sketch pens of different colours

experiments.safety: If the child stands on a chair to drop, a grown-up holds the chair. Dropping from the child's own raised hand is high enough.

schedule.what: Cut two paper leaves. Crumple one. Drop each one ten times and mark where it lands.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table with a tick for inside and a cross for outside. Count the ticks for the ball and for the leaf. Draw the newspaper with all the crosses on it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the paper leaf test. You make the paper leaf and the paper ball.
flow.do: 1. Fold the notebook paper in half. 2. Draw a leaf about as long as your child's hand on it. 3. Cut through both layers, so you get two leaves the same size. 4. Your child crumples one leaf into a tight ball.
flow.say: These two leaves came from the same paper, and they are the same size. So they weigh the same. Now crumple one into a tight ball. Keep the other one flat.
flow.kid: Cut two paper leaves the same size. Crumple one into a ball. Keep one flat.
flow.parent: Folding the paper before cutting gives two leaves of exactly the same size and weight. That makes it a fair test.

flow.context: In this step of the paper leaf test, you set up the target and guess.
flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan and close the windows. 2. Lay two sheets of newspaper side by side on the floor. 3. Put a steel plate in the middle and draw around it. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: We will drop each one ten times, from up high, over the middle of the circle. Which one will land inside the circle more often? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will drop each one ten times over the circle. Which lands inside more often? Why?

ask.q: Which one will land inside the circle more often? Why?
good: The ball, because it is round and falls straight.
The leaf, because it is flat and floats down slowly.
The same, because they weigh the same.

flow.parent: Write down your child's guess and reason. Do not say who is right. Many children think that the same weight means the same fall.

flow.context: In this step of the paper leaf test, you drop the paper ball ten times.
flow.do: 1. Your child stands beside the circle and holds the ball high, arm straight up, over the middle. 2. Let go. Do not throw. 3. Mark where it first lands with a red cross. 4. Pick it up and do it again, ten times in all.
flow.say: Hold it high over the middle of the circle. Just open your fingers. Don't throw it. Where did it land? Make a red cross there.
flow.kid: Hold the ball high over the circle. Open your fingers. Mark where it lands.
flow.parent: Mark the spot where it first touches the paper, even if it bounces a little. Most drops land inside or close to the circle.

flow.context: In this step of the paper leaf test, you drop the flat paper leaf ten times.
flow.do: 1. Your child holds the flat leaf by the tip, flat side down, high over the middle of the circle. 2. Let go. 3. Mark where it comes to rest with a blue cross. 4. Do it ten times in all, holding it the same way each time.
flow.say: Now the flat leaf. Hold it flat, by the tip, in the same place. Let go. Watch how it falls. Make a blue cross where it lands.
flow.kid: Hold the flat leaf the same way each time. Let go. Watch it fall. Mark where it lands.

ask.q: How did the leaf fall? Was it the same as the ball?
good: It swung from side to side.
It turned over and slid sideways.
It fell slowly, and the ball fell fast.

flow.parent: The leaf usually swings, turns or slides, and lands somewhere new each time, often outside the circle. If a leaf lands off the newspaper, put a cross at the edge closest to it.

flow.context: This is the last step of the paper leaf test. You count and say what you found.
flow.do: 1. Count the red crosses inside the circle. 2. Count the blue crosses inside the circle. 3. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. 4. Then read the card on why a falling leaf never lands in the same place twice.
flow.say: How many red crosses are inside the circle? How many blue ones? Did the leaf ever land in the same place twice? Why do you think the ball and the leaf were so different?
flow.kid: Count the red crosses inside. Count the blue ones. Why were they so different?

ask.q: Why did the ball land near the same spot, but the leaf did not?
good: The air pushed on the flat leaf and made it swing.
The ball is small and round, so the air cannot push it much.
Each time the leaf started a bit differently.

check.q: The paper ball and the paper leaf weighed the same. Why did the leaf land in a new place each time?
options: The air pushed on its big flat side and made it swing
Gravity does not pull on flat things
check.why: They weighed the same, so weight was not the difference. The air pushed on the leaf's big flat side, and tiny changes in each drop sent it somewhere new. Gravity pulls on both.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the crosses as evidence: the red ones are bunched, the blue ones are spread out. Then it gives a reason about the shape and the air.

experiments.title: The Splash Test: is any splash the same as another?
experiments.context: In this experiment you let drops of yellow haldi water fall onto white paper. You drop them from the same height and look at each splash. Then you drop from higher up.
experiments.question: If the same kind of drop falls from the same height, will its splash look the same each time?
experiments.predict: We will drop four drops from the same height. Will the four splashes look the same? Will a drop from higher up make a bigger or smaller splash? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same haldi water, the same dropper and the same paper every time. For the first four drops we use the same height, measured with a ruler. Only the height changes for the last drops.
results_table: Number of little dots around it

materials.item: a pinch of haldi in half a small cup of water, or a few drops of ink in water
a medicine dropper, or a drinking straw
newspaper to put under the paper

experiments.safety: Haldi stains clothes and the floor. Wear old clothes and work on newspaper.

schedule.what: Drop haldi water from the same height four times, then from higher up. Compare the splashes.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw a circle around each splash and write its height beside it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the splash test. You get ready and guess.
flow.do: 1. Stir a pinch of haldi into half a small cup of water. 2. Spread newspaper on the floor and put a white sheet on top. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: We will drop four drops of this yellow water from the same height. Will the four splashes look the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four drops will fall from the same height. Will the splashes look the same? Why?

ask.q: Will the four splashes look the same? Why?
good: Yes, because it is the same water and the same height.
No, because splashes are always different.

flow.parent: Write down the guess and the reason. No need to say who is right.

flow.context: In this step of the splash test, you make four splashes from the same height.
flow.do: 1. Stand the ruler up on the paper. 2. Your child fills the dropper and holds its tip at the top of the ruler, 30 cm up. 3. Squeeze gently until one drop falls. 4. Move to a new part of the paper and do it again, four times in all.
flow.say: Hold the dropper at the top of the ruler. Squeeze very gently, so just one drop falls. Look at the splash. Now make another one next to it.
flow.kid: Hold the dropper at the top of the ruler. Squeeze gently. Look at the splash.
flow.parent: With a straw, dip one end in the water, put a finger on the top end and lift it out. Lift your finger a little to let one drop go. Each drop makes a yellow spot with some little dots around it.

flow.context: In this step of the splash test, you look closely at the four splashes and count.
flow.do: 1. Your child counts the little dots around each splash. 2. Write the numbers in the table. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Count the little dots around each splash. Are the numbers the same? Are the dots in the same places?
flow.kid: Count the little dots around each splash. Are any two splashes the same?

ask.q: Are any two splashes exactly the same?
good: No. One has 4 dots and one has 7.
No. The dots are in different places.
They are nearly the same size, but the dots are different.

flow.parent: The middle spots are often about the same size, but the little dots around them differ in number and place. That is what to notice.

flow.context: In this step of the splash test, a grown-up drops a drop from much higher.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up stands and holds the dropper about one metre above a clean part of the paper. 2. Let one drop fall. 3. Your child counts the dots around it.
flow.say: Now I will drop one from much higher up. What will it look like? Let's count its dots.
flow.kid: Watch the drop from high up. Count the dots around its splash.
flow.parent: A drop from about one metre hits much harder. It usually spreads wider, with more spikes and dots around it. Aim carefully, or the drop may miss the paper.

flow.context: This is the last step of the splash test. You say what you found.
flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. 2. Then read the card on why no two splashes are the same.
flow.say: It was the same water and the same height. Why do you think the splashes were not all the same? Why was the high one different?
flow.kid: Same water, same height. Why were the splashes different?

good: Each drop was a bit different.
The paper is a bit bumpy.
The high drop hit harder, so it spread more.

flow.parent: Any reason about tiny differences in the drop or the paper is a good start. The card explains the rest.

activities.title: Shake and Tip: can the beans land the same way twice?
activities.context: In this activity you shake ten rajma beans in a tumbler and tip them onto a plate, twice. Then you put them in a neat row. You notice which way you can make again.

materials.item: ten rajma beans, or ten chana, buttons or small pebbles
a steel tumbler and a steel plate

schedule.what: Shake and tip ten beans twice and draw them. Then line them up in a row.

activities.record: Draw the beans after the first tip, after the second tip and in the neat row.

setup.art: A child's hand covering the top of a steel tumbler with ten rajma beans inside, shaking it.
setup.caption: 1. Put ten beans in a tumbler. Cover it and shake.

setup.art: Rajma beans scattered unevenly across a steel plate next to a tipped tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Tip them onto a plate. Draw where they are.

setup.art: Ten rajma beans in a straight neat row on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 3. Line them up in a row.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts ten beans in the tumbler, covers it with a hand and shakes it. 2. Tip the beans onto the plate. 3. Your child draws where they landed.
flow.say: Shake the tumbler and tip the beans onto the plate. Look at where they landed. Draw them quickly.
flow.kid: Shake the beans. Tip them out. Draw where they landed.
flow.parent: This is the thing to notice first. Do not explain anything yet.

flow.do: 1. Put the beans back in the tumbler. 2. Before tipping, ask the question below. 3. Shake and tip again, and compare with the drawing.
flow.say: Can you make them land in exactly the same places as last time? Try it. Look at your drawing. Is it the same?
flow.kid: Can the beans land the same way again? Try it. Look at your drawing.

ask.q: Did the beans land the same way as last time?
good: No, they are in different places.
Some are close, but not the same.

flow.parent: They will not land the same way. That is the point to notice.

flow.do: 1. Your child lines the ten beans up in a straight row. 2. Mix them up, and ask your child to make the row again.
flow.say: Now put them in a straight row. Now I mix them up. Can you make the row again? Which way could you make the same twice, the row or the heap?
flow.kid: Line the beans up in a row. Can you make the row again?

ask.q: Which could you make the same again, the row or the heap? Why?
good: The row, because I know the rule: one after another in a line.
Not the heap, because nobody decides where each bean goes.

flow.think: What rule did you use to make the row?
flow.parent: The row has order: there is a rule, so it can be made again. The heap is messy: no rule we can use decides where each bean goes.

activities.title: Draw a Kolam: a pattern with a rule
activities.context: In this activity you draw a simple kolam on paper. You make a grid of dots and loop a line around them. Then you draw it a second time and see if it comes out the same.

materials.item: two sheets of paper, or a doorstep and rice flour or chalk
a pencil, or a sketch pen

schedule.what: Make a grid of nine dots. Draw a kolam around them. Then draw it again.

activities.record: Keep both kolams side by side. Write the rule you used under them.

setup.art: Nine dots in three rows of three on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Make three rows of three dots.

setup.art: A single line looping around each of the nine dots, without touching any of them, making a simple kolam.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a line that goes around every dot without touching it.

setup.art: Two matching kolams side by side on paper.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the same kolam again next to it.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes three rows of three dots, evenly spaced, about two fingers apart.
flow.say: Make three rows of three dots. Keep them the same distance apart. That is the start of a kolam.
flow.kid: Make three rows of three dots. Keep them the same distance apart.

flow.do: 1. Show the rule: the line goes around each dot and never touches a dot. 2. Your child draws a line that loops around all nine dots, joining up where it started. 3. Any loop pattern is fine, as long as the rule is kept.
flow.say: Here is the rule. The line goes around every dot. It never touches a dot. Can you make one line that goes around all nine?
flow.kid: The line goes around every dot. It never touches a dot. Try it.
flow.parent: A simple shape to start with: draw a wavy line that weaves between the rows, then join it up at the ends. If it goes wrong, start again on new dots. It takes a few tries.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes nine new dots next to the first kolam. 2. Draws the same kolam again. 3. Compare the two.
flow.say: Now draw the same kolam again, next to the first one. Is it the same? How did you know where the line goes?
flow.kid: Draw the same kolam again. Is it the same? How did you know?

ask.q: How could you draw the same kolam again?
good: Because I know the rule.
Because the dots show me where the line goes.

flow.parent: The second kolam should look much like the first. Order means there is a rule, so the same thing can be made again. Compare this with the beans or the falling leaf.

activities.title: Drip Watch: drops from a tap
activities.context: In this activity you let a kitchen tap drip slowly into a steel plate. You watch the drops and the splashes, and see if any two are alike.

materials.item: a kitchen tap and a steel plate or a bucket lid

schedule.what: Let a tap drip slowly onto a steel plate. Watch and listen to each drop.

activities.record: Draw two splashes you saw. Write one way they were different.

setup.art: A kitchen tap turned on so it drips slowly onto a steel plate in the sink.
setup.caption: 1. Turn the tap on so it just drips.

setup.art: A child's face close to the sink, watching a drop splash on the steel plate.
setup.caption: 2. Watch each drop splash.

flow.do: 1. Put a steel plate in the sink under the tap. 2. Turn the tap on so it drips slowly, about one drop each second.
flow.say: Watch the drops. Listen too. Does every drop make the same splash and the same sound?
flow.kid: Watch each drop. Listen. Is every splash the same?

good: The drops come at about the same time, but the splashes look different.
Some splash higher than others.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below. 2. Turn off the tap. Save the water in the plate for a plant.
flow.say: The drops fall at about the same speed, one after the other. That part has a pattern. But do the splashes? Which part is neat, and which part is messy?
flow.kid: The drops come one after another. Do the splashes look the same too?

ask.q: Which part is neat and which part is messy?
good: The drips are neat, one after another.
The splashes are messy, each one different.

flow.parent: Many dripping taps drip with a steady beat, but each splash is different. Use the water for a plant afterwards so none is wasted.

games.title: Same Again or Never Twice? a card game
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or 1 player sorting alone
games.context: This is a quick card game. Each card shows something that happens. You decide if it can happen the same way again, or if it never happens the same way twice.

items.f: A paper ball dropped over a circle
items.b: Same again. It lands near the same spot every time.

items.f: A dry leaf falling from a tree
items.b: Never twice. The air pushes it somewhere new.

items.f: A kolam drawn around nine dots
items.b: Same again. Follow the rule and draw it again.

items.f: A raindrop splashing on a step
items.b: Never twice. Each splash breaks into different dots.

items.f: Pencils lined up from short to long
items.b: Same again. The rule tells you where each pencil goes.

items.f: Rajma beans tipped out of a tumbler
items.b: Never twice. They land in a new heap each time.

items.f: The Sun rising in the east
items.b: Same again. It rises in the east every morning.

items.f: The shape of a cloud
items.b: Never twice. Clouds keep changing shape.

items.f: A clap pattern: clap, clap, stamp
items.b: Same again. Anyone who knows the pattern can copy it.

items.f: Smoke curling up from an agarbatti
items.b: Never twice. The smoke swirls a new way each moment.

items.f: Steel tumblers stacked one inside another
items.b: Same again. Each one fits inside the next.

items.f: Milk splashing as it is poured
items.b: Never twice. Every splash is different.

items.f: A saree border: red, blue, red, blue
items.b: Same again. The pattern repeats.

items.f: A feather drifting down
items.b: Never twice. The air pushes the light feather about.

items.f: A clock ticking every second
items.b: Same again. It ticks at the same beat.

items.f: Waves on the beach at Marina in Chennai
items.b: Never twice. No two waves are exactly the same.

rules: Cut out the 16 happening cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
Each player gets two sign cards: 'Same again' and 'Never twice'.
One player turns over the top card and reads it out.
Everyone holds up one sign at the same time.
Turn the card over and read the back. Everyone who was right gets a point.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone, sort the cards into two piles and then check the backs.

setup.art: A pile of small cards face down, and two children each holding two sign cards that say 'Same again' and 'Never twice'.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the cards. Each player takes two signs.

setup.art: A girl reading a card that says 'A dry leaf falling from a tree', while two children hold up 'Never twice'.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Hold up a sign.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Read the rules out loud.
flow.say: Each card is something that happens. If it can happen the same way again, hold up 'Same again'. If it never happens the same way twice, hold up 'Never twice'.
flow.kid: Read the card. Can it happen the same way again? Hold up a sign.

flow.do: 1. Take turns reading a card. 2. Everyone holds up a sign. 3. Read the back and give points.
flow.say: A feather drifting down. Same again, or never twice? Hold up your sign. Why did you choose that?
flow.kid: Read a card. Hold up a sign. Check the back.

ask.q: Why does a feather never fall the same way twice?
good: The air pushes on it a lot.
It is light and flat, like the paper leaf.

check.q: Which of these can happen the same way again?
options: A kolam drawn around nine dots
A leaf falling from a tree
check.why: A kolam follows a rule, so it can be drawn the same way again. Splashes and falling leaves are different every time.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the 'Never twice' cards. Do they follow rules too, or is it all luck?
flow.kid: Look at the 'Never twice' cards. Do they follow rules too?

ask.q: Do the 'Never twice' things follow rules?
good: Yes. Gravity pulls the leaf down every time.
Yes, but tiny changes make them different.

games.title: Copy My Clap: a rhythm game
games.context: This is a clapping game. One player claps a pattern and the others copy it. Then the leader drums freely, with no pattern, and the others try to copy that too.

items.f: Clap, clap, stamp
items.b: A pattern of 3 beats. Repeat it 4 times.

items.f: Clap, stamp, clap, stamp
items.b: A pattern of 2 beats. Repeat it 4 times.

items.f: Clap, clap, clap, pat your knees
items.b: A pattern of 4 beats. Repeat it 3 times.

items.f: Stamp, clap, clap
items.b: A pattern of 3 beats. Repeat it 4 times.

items.f: Free drumming
items.b: No pattern. Drum on your knees any way you like for 5 seconds.

items.f: Free drumming
items.b: No pattern. Drum on the floor any way you like for 5 seconds.

rules: Cut out the 6 pattern cards. Shuffle them and put them face down.
The leader takes a card and does what it says.
The other players copy it straight after.
If everyone copies it exactly, they get a point each.
Take turns being the leader until the cards are finished.

setup.art: A girl clapping her hands while two children watch, ready to copy.
setup.caption: 1. The leader claps the pattern on the card.

setup.art: Two children clapping together, copying the leader.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone copies it.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Read the rules out loud.
flow.say: The leader claps what the card says. Then we copy it. Let's see which ones we can copy exactly.
flow.kid: Watch the leader. Then copy the clap exactly.

flow.do: 1. Take turns as leader. 2. Copy each card. 3. Give points.
flow.say: Clap, clap, stamp. Clap, clap, stamp. Your turn. Now free drumming. Can you copy that?
flow.kid: Copy the leader's clap. Can you copy the free drumming too?

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which ones were easy to copy, and which were hard? Why?
flow.kid: Which claps were easy to copy? Which were hard? Why?

ask.q: Why was the pattern easy to copy, but the free drumming hard?
good: The pattern has a rule that repeats.
The free drumming had no rule, so I could not remember it.

flow.parent: A pattern has order, so it can be repeated. Free drumming has no pattern, like the beans on the plate.

projects.title: My Never-Twice Diary: three days of watching
projects.context: In this project you keep a small diary for three days. Each day, you find one thing that happens the same way every time, and one thing that never happens the same way twice.

materials.item: three sheets of paper folded into a little book, or three pages of a notebook

schedule.what: Find and draw one thing that happens the same way every time, and one that never does.
Look out of the window at the sky. Draw the clouds in the morning and again in the evening.
Find two new things in the kitchen. Then read the whole diary and choose your favourite page.

projects.record: Each page has two boxes: 'Same every time' and 'Never twice'. Draw one thing in each box and write one word about it.

setup.art: A small homemade booklet with three pages, each split into two boxes labelled 'Same every time' and 'Never twice'.
setup.caption: 1. Make a little book with three pages.

setup.art: A page with a clock drawn in one box and a cloud drawn in the other.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, draw one thing in each box.

flow.do: 1. Fold three sheets into a little book. 2. Draw two boxes on each page. 3. Your child finds and draws one thing for each box.
flow.say: Today, find one thing that happens the same way every time, and one thing that never does. Look around the house.
flow.kid: Find one thing that is the same every time. Find one that never is. Draw them.

flow.do: 1. In the morning, your child draws the clouds from a window. 2. In the evening, draws them again.
flow.say: Look out of the window. Draw the clouds. We will look again this evening. Will they be the same?
flow.kid: Draw the clouds this morning. Look again this evening. Are they the same?

ask.q: Were the clouds the same in the evening?
good: No, they changed shape.
The sky was clear in the evening.

flow.parent: If you cannot see the sky, a grown-up can hold a pot of hot water. Your child watches the steam from a safe distance. It also never moves the same way twice.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds two new things in the kitchen. 2. Then reads the whole diary aloud.
flow.say: Find two things in the kitchen today. Then let's read your whole diary. Which page do you like best?
flow.kid: Find two things in the kitchen. Then read your diary. Which page is best?

ask.q: What did you find in the kitchen?
good: Steel tumblers stacked the same every time.
Mustard seeds popping in oil, never the same way.
Rice grains falling into a pot.

challenges.title: The Landing Challenge: make a flat paper land on the target
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A flat paper leaf lands in a new place every time. Without crumpling it, can you change it so it lands inside the circle more often?
challenges.problem: Change a flat paper leaf so that it lands inside the plate circle as often as possible, without crumpling it into a ball.
constraints: Use a paper leaf the same size as in the paper leaf test.
Do not crumple it into a ball.
You may fold it, add one paper clip, or cut it.
Drop it from the same height each time, ten times.
materials: paper leaves cut from notebook paper
the newspaper with the plate circle from the paper leaf test
crayons to mark where it lands
general: Clip a paper clip to the tip. The heavy tip goes down first, so the leaf falls more straight.
Fold the leaf in half along the middle, like a V. Does it swing less?
creative: Fold the leaf into a cone, like a small paper cup turned upside down.
Fold the leaf in half twice, to make a small thick square.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own leaf design. Drop it ten times and count how many land inside the circle. Can you beat the flat leaf's score?

setup.art: Three paper leaves on a table: one flat, one with a paper clip on the tip and one folded into a V.
setup.caption: 1. Change your paper leaf in your own way.

setup.art: A child dropping a paper leaf with a paper clip on its tip over a circle on newspaper.
setup.caption: 2. Drop it ten times. Count how many land in the circle.

flow.do: 1. Remind your child of the flat leaf's score from the paper leaf test. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: The flat leaf landed in a new place each time. We cannot crumple it. How could we change it so it lands in the circle more often?
flow.kid: How could you change the flat leaf so it lands in the circle?

ask.q: How could you make it land in the circle more often?
good: Make the tip heavier.
Fold it so it is not so flat.
Make it smaller.

flow.do: 1. Your child changes a new leaf in their own way. 2. Drops it ten times from the same height. 3. Counts how many land inside the circle. 4. Tries one more design.
flow.say: Make your design. Drop it ten times from the same height. Count how many land inside the circle.
flow.kid: Make your design. Drop it ten times. Count how many land inside.
flow.parent: A paper clip on the tip often makes the leaf dive tip first, so it lands closer to the circle. A cone or a thick folded square may fall straighter too. Some designs will not work, and that is part of the test.

flow.do: 1. Compare the scores. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which design landed in the circle most often? Why do you think it worked?
flow.kid: Which design was best? Why do you think it worked?

ask.q: Why did your best design work?
good: The clip made the front heavy, so it went down tip first.
Folding stopped it swinging so much.

flow.parent: Designs that stop the leaf swinging make it easier to predict. That is why a seed like a coconut drops straight, but a light, winged seed drifts far.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: something that repeats the same way
the force that pulls things down
say what will happen before it happens
items.why: These are the four words the child needs to talk about the tests. Order and pattern are about rules. Gravity is the pull down. Predict is saying what comes next.

items.p: In the paper leaf test, which one landed inside the circle most often?
items.why: The ball fell almost straight down, because the air could not push it about much. Choosing 'both the same' means thinking that the same weight gives the same fall. The test shows shape matters too.
items.context: This question is about the paper leaf test. You dropped a flat paper leaf and a crumpled paper ball ten times each, from the same height, and marked where each one landed.

items.p: Sort these into 'can happen the same way again' and 'never happens the same way twice'.
items: pencils lined up from short to long
items.why: The kolam, the pencil line and the clap pattern all follow a rule you can repeat. The leaf, the splash and the cloud follow rules too, but tiny changes make them different every time.

items.p: Draw the newspaper from your paper leaf test. Put a red cross where the ball landed and a blue cross where the leaf landed.
items.a: Red crosses bunched in or near the circle, and blue crosses spread out all over the paper.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference clearly: the red crosses close together, the blue ones far apart. That spread is the evidence that the leaf lands in a new place each time.
items.context: This question is about the paper leaf test. You dropped a flat paper leaf and a crumpled paper ball ten times each, from the same height, and marked where each one landed.
items.art: An empty rectangle for the newspaper with a circle in the middle.

items.p: The paper ball and the flat paper leaf weighed the same.
items.why: True. Both were cut from the same folded paper, the same size. So weight cannot be why they fell differently. Their shape was different.
items.context: This question is about the paper leaf test. You dropped a flat paper leaf and a crumpled paper ball ten times each, from the same height, and marked where each one landed.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the flat leaf swing from side to side as it fell?
items.a: The air pushed on its big flat side, so it swung and slid instead of falling straight down.
items.why: A strong answer names the air pushing on the flat side. Saying 'because it is paper' is not enough, because the ball was paper too.
items.context: This question is about the paper leaf test. You dropped a flat paper leaf and a crumpled paper ball ten times each, from the same height, and marked where each one landed.

items.p: Divya dropped her paper ball 10 times. 9 landed inside the circle. How many landed outside?
items.why: 10 take away 9 is 1. So only 1 drop landed outside the circle. The ball was easy to predict.
items.context: This question is about the paper leaf test. You dropped a flat paper leaf and a crumpled paper ball ten times each, from the same height, and marked where each one landed.

items.p: Label the arrows on the falling leaf: 'gravity pulls down' and 'air pushes up'.
a: arrow pointing down: gravity pulls down
arrow pointing up: air pushes up
items.why: Gravity pulls every falling thing down. The air pushes back against it. On a flat leaf, the air's push is big, so the leaf falls slowly and swings.
items.art: A paper leaf with one arrow pointing down below it and one arrow pointing up from under it, each with an empty label line.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 2, and his older sister Meenakshi watch a dry leaf fall from a tree.

views.says: Nobody can say where it will land, so it is just luck. No rules decide it.
Gravity pulls it and the air pushes it every time. So rules decide where it lands.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For example, agreeing with Meenakshi because gravity and air push on the leaf the same way each time. It also says Arjun is right that nobody can predict where it lands.
items.why: Both have a point. The leaf follows rules, but tiny changes make it impossible to predict. A strong answer uses the paper leaf test as evidence.

items.p: Three of these follow a pattern you can repeat. Which one does not?
items.why: Every rain splash is different, so it cannot be repeated. The beads, the clap and the kolam all follow a rule.

items.p: Put the paper leaf test in order.
items: Cut two leaves the same size
Drop each one ten times over the circle
Count the crosses inside the circle
items.why: First you make two leaves that weigh the same. Then you make one into a ball. Then you drop and mark, and last you count to compare.
items.context: This question is about the paper leaf test. You dropped a flat paper leaf and a crumpled paper ball ten times each, from the same height, and marked where each one landed.

items.p: In the splash test, which drop made the most little dots around its splash?
items.why: A drop from higher up hits harder. It spreads further and breaks into more little dots. Choosing "the same number" means thinking that the splash does not care how far the drop falls.
items.context: This question is about the splash test. You let drops of yellow haldi water fall onto white paper from the same height, and looked at each splash.

items.p: The water and the height were the same. Why were the four splashes still different?
items.a: Each drop wobbles a little as it falls, and the paper has tiny bumps. These tiny differences change where the splash breaks into little dots.
items.why: A strong answer names a tiny difference we cannot see, such as the wobble of the drop or bumps on the paper. Saying 'by luck' does not say what made them different.
items.context: This question is about the splash test. You let drops of yellow haldi water fall onto white paper from the same height, and looked at each splash.

items.p: Draw a splash from 30 centimetres and a splash from one metre. Show how they were different.
items.a: A small splash with a few little dots, and a bigger splash with more spikes and many more dots.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the high drop spreading wider with more dots, because it hit the paper harder.
items.context: This question is about the splash test. You let drops of yellow haldi water fall onto white paper from the same height, and looked at each splash.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, one labelled 30 centimetres and one labelled 1 metre.

items.p: Lakshmi and her Amma are drawing a kolam. Their neighbour, Fatima Aunty, is watching the rain.

views.says: Neat things like a kolam are better, because we can make them again.
Messy things like rain and clouds are better, because they are always new.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For example, agreeing with Lakshmi because you can plan with order. It also says what Fatima Aunty has right: messy things bring surprises and are never boring.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Order lets us repeat and plan. Chaos brings new things every time. A strong answer sees what each side gets right.

items.p: If something is messy, no rules are at work on it.
items.why: False. A falling leaf and a splash look messy, but gravity and the air follow the same rules every time. Tiny changes make them hard to predict.

items.p: Sort these by what decides how they fall: 'falls nearly straight' or 'swings and drifts'.
items.why: Heavy or round things push through the air and fall nearly straight. Light, flat things are pushed a lot by the air, so they swing and drift.

items.p: Kavya dropped a flat paper leaf 10 times. 2 landed inside the circle. Her paper ball landed inside 9 times. How many more times did the ball land inside?
items.why: 9 take away 2 is 7. The ball landed inside 7 more times than the leaf, because the air pushed the flat leaf about.
items.context: This question is about the paper leaf test. You dropped a flat paper leaf and a crumpled paper ball ten times each, from the same height, and marked where each one landed.

items.p: Many people think a flat leaf and a paper ball should fall the same way, because they weigh the same. What would you show them to change their mind?
items.a: I would show them the paper leaf test: two pieces of the same paper, one flat and one crumpled, dropped ten times each. The ball lands near the same spot, and the leaf lands all over the place.
items.why: A strong answer describes a fair test with the same weight, and says what result would show that shape matters.

items.p: Look at the kolam. Label the dot, the line and the rule.
a: dot: the dots in the grid
line: the white line looping around the dots
rule: the line goes around every dot and never touches it
items.why: A kolam has order because it follows a rule. The dots show where the line goes, and the rule says how it goes around them.
items.art: A simple kolam of nine dots with a looping line, with three empty label lines pointing to a dot, the line and a space underneath for the rule.

items.p: Weather follows rules of air, water and heat. Why can't weather scientists say exactly what the weather will be a month from now?
opts: Weather has no rules at all
Tiny changes in the air grow bigger over time
items.why: Weather is chaotic, like the falling leaf. Tiny changes in the air grow over the days. Choosing 'no rules at all' mixes up hard to predict with having no rules.

quiz.why: Order means there is a rule, so you can say where each thing goes. A heap has no rule we can use.

quiz.p: Which of these is a pattern?
opts: Rajma beans tipped onto a plate
Clap, clap, stamp, clap, clap, stamp
quiz.why: A pattern repeats in the same way. Clap, clap, stamp repeats. The beans and the cloud never repeat.

quiz.p: Divya drops a crumpled paper ball ten times from the same height. Where does it land?
opts: Near the same spot every time
In a new place far away each time
quiz.why: The air cannot push the small round ball about much, so it falls nearly straight down every time.

quiz.p: Divya drops a flat paper leaf ten times from the same height. Where does it land?
opts: In exactly the same spot every time
In a new place each time
Always in the middle of the circle
quiz.why: The air pushes on the flat leaf and makes it swing. Tiny changes in each drop send it somewhere new.

quiz.p: Which two forces act on a falling leaf?
opts: Gravity pulling down and air pushing back
quiz.why: Gravity pulls every falling thing down. The air pushes back against it as it falls. Even with no wind, the air still pushes.

quiz.p: Why can't you make a flat paper leaf land in the same place twice?
opts: The rules of falling change every time
You can never let go of it in exactly the same way, and the air moves a tiny bit
quiz.why: The rules stay the same. What changes are tiny things, like your fingers and the air. On a flat leaf, those tiny changes grow into a big difference.

quiz.p: Sreeja drops four drops of haldi water from the same height onto paper. What will she see?
opts: Four splashes, each a little different
quiz.why: Each drop wobbles a little and the paper has tiny bumps, so each splash breaks into dots in its own way.

quiz.p: A drop falls from much higher up. What does its splash look like?
opts: Bigger, with more dots around it
Exactly the same as a low drop
quiz.why: A drop from higher up hits harder. It spreads further and breaks into more little dots.

quiz.p: A splash looks messy. Does it follow rules?
opts: Yes, the water follows the same rules every time
No, messy things have no rules
quiz.why: Messy does not mean there are no rules. The water always falls and spreads out by the same rules. Tiny changes make each splash different.

quiz.p: Scientists call things that follow rules but never happen the same way twice by a special name. What is it?
quiz.why: Chaos is the word for things like falling leaves and weather. They follow rules, but tiny changes at the start make big changes at the end.

quiz.p: Is anything in the world truly random, with nothing at all deciding how it comes out?
quiz.why: Some scientists think the tiniest particles are truly random. Others think there may be hidden rules. Nobody has settled this yet.

applications: Weather scientists at the India Meteorological Department use the rules of air, water and heat to say what the weather will probably be in the next few days. Weather is chaotic, so they cannot say exactly what it will be weeks ahead.
Kolam and rangoli makers use rules of dots and lines, so the same design can be drawn again and taught to others.
People who make parachutes and fold paper planes change the shape to control how things fall through the air.
Some scientists film raindrops hitting leaves very fast. They want to see how splashes carry plant germs from one leaf to the next.
Shopkeepers stack fruit and steel vessels in neat order, so they can find things fast and count them easily.

open_questions.q: Is anything in the world truly random?
open_questions.why_open: The tiniest particles seem to behave by chance. Some physicists think this chance is real. Others think there are hidden rules we have not found. Nobody has settled it.

open_questions.q: How far ahead could the weather ever be predicted?
open_questions.why_open: Weather forecasts have got much better, but tiny changes in the air grow over time. Scientists still argue about how many days ahead a forecast could ever be useful.

open_questions.q: Why do our eyes and minds like to find order?
open_questions.why_open: People often see patterns, like faces in clouds, even where there is no pattern. Scientists are still finding out why minds do this.

maths.problem: In the paper leaf test, Divya kept a tally for the paper ball. Inside the circle she made one group of 5 marks and one group of 4 marks. Outside she made 1 mark. How many drops did she make?
maths.explain: 5 and 4 make 9, so 9 drops landed inside. 1 landed outside. 9 and 1 make 10.
maths.context: This question is about the paper leaf test. You dropped a flat paper leaf and a crumpled paper ball ten times each, from the same height, and marked where each one landed.
maths.why_maths: A tally helps you keep count while you drop, so you do not lose track.

maths.problem: Divya's paper ball landed inside the circle 9 times out of 10. Her flat leaf landed inside 2 times out of 10. If she drops the leaf once more, is it likely or unlikely to land inside?
maths.explain: The leaf landed inside only 2 times out of 10, and outside 8 times. So it is unlikely to land inside next time. But it could, because sometimes it did.
maths.context: This question is about the paper leaf test. You dropped a flat paper leaf and a crumpled paper ball ten times each, from the same height, and marked where each one landed.
maths.why_maths: We cannot predict one leaf drop, but counting many drops tells us what is likely.

maths.problem: Nila draws a kolam border with a pattern: big loop, small loop, small loop, big loop, small loop, small loop. What are the next three loops?
maths.answer: Big loop, small loop, small loop.
maths.explain: The pattern repeats every three loops: big, small, small. So after the second small loop, it starts again with big, small, small.
maths.context: This question is about the kolam activity, where you drew a line looping around a grid of dots by following a rule.
maths.why_maths: A pattern has order, so maths can tell you what comes next.

maths.problem: In the splash test, Sreeja's four splashes from 30 cm had 4, 7, 3 and 5 little dots. Her splash from one metre had 14. Which splash from 30 cm had the most dots? How many more did the high splash have than that one?
maths.answer: The splash with 7 dots had the most. The high splash had 7 more.
maths.explain: 7 is bigger than 4, 3 and 5. 14 take away 7 is 7. So even the busiest low splash had only half as many dots as the high one.
maths.context: This question is about the splash test. You let drops of yellow haldi water fall onto white paper from the same height, and looked at each splash.
maths.why_maths: Comparing numbers shows that the high drop really made a bigger splash, not just a different one.

roots.context: We have dropped paper leaves and paper balls, made splashes and drawn a kolam. Now we ask what neat and messy things tell us about the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Your paper ball landed near the same spot every time, but your flat leaf landed somewhere new each time. Both followed the same rules: gravity pulled them down, and the air pushed against them. The air pushed the light, flat leaf so much that tiny changes in each drop sent it somewhere new. So something can follow exact rules and still never happen the same way twice.
deep_truth.habit: We think that when something is messy or cannot be predicted, no rules are at work and it is just luck. The paper leaf followed exactly the same rules as the ball, every time.
deep_truth.evidence: In the paper leaf test, two pieces of the same paper, with the same weight, were dropped the same way. The ball's crosses were bunched in the circle. The leaf's crosses were spread across the newspaper.

three.who_am_i: Every breath you take is a little different from the last one. You follow the same rules of your body each day, and still no two days of you are the same.
three.what_is_life: A plant grows each new leaf by the same rules. Still, each leaf has its own small bends and curves.
three.what_is_this_world: Clouds, rivers, waves and falling leaves all follow rules. Yet the world never happens the same way twice.

roots.thread: A few rules, like gravity and the push of the air, act on every falling leaf and every drop. From those same rules come many different landings and splashes, and no two are alike. Everything is conscious, the moving air and the falling water too, each meeting the world in their own way. Many scientists disagree, and say only living things with brains can be aware.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker from about 500 BCE, as reported by Plato in the Cratylus, 402a
teachings.teaching: Heraclitus said that you cannot step twice into the same river. The water you stepped into has already flowed on, and new water has come.
teachings.link: The river follows the same rules every day, but it is never the same water twice. Your paper leaf and your splashes were like that too: the same rules, but a new result each time.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught that everything made of parts keeps changing. Nothing made stays the same.
teachings.link: A splash lasts a moment and is gone, and the next one is different. A cloud keeps changing shape too.

science.text: Things that follow exact rules can still be impossible to predict, because tiny changes at the start grow into big changes. Scientists call this chaos. Weather is chaotic.
Whether anything in nature is truly random, with nothing at all deciding it, is still argued about by physicists.

other_view.who: Pierre-Simon Laplace, a French scientist, in 1814, and many people since
other_view.view: If we knew everything about the leaf and the air, we could predict exactly where it would land. So 'never the same twice' is only about what we know, not about the world. Many also say air and water have no awareness at all.

practice.title: Three drops

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat. The paper leaf test needs only notebook paper, newspaper, a plate and crayons. Two leaves cut from folded paper weigh the same. With the fan off, a crumpled ball dropped from a child's raised hand lands in or near a plate-sized circle almost every time. A flat palm-sized paper leaf swings and slides and usually lands well outside it, often 20 to 60 centimetres away, so the spread of crosses is easy to see. In the splash test, haldi water from a dropper or straw makes clear yellow spots with a few little dots around them from 30 centimetres, and wider, spikier splashes from about one metre.
